archetype.name: Pocket Passer (timing-and-rhythm)
archetype.definition: A rhythm thrower who wins from a clean pocket with anticipation into the intermediate zone and play-action windows, producing big efficiency when protected and little with his legs.

report.headline: Downfield bounce-back season, but the shots dried up as interceptions crept in
report.take:
Goff is the same quarterback he has been for a decade: a pocket thrower who lives on timing and the intermediate middle of the field, scrambles almost never (7 times all year), and gives nothing as a runner (1.4 yards a carry, mostly sneaks and kneels). What changed in 2026 is how far he has been willing to push it. His aggressiveness is 15.36%, up 2.9 points on last year, and his intended air yards sit near 8, above the 6.8 aDOT he posted in both 2024 and 2025. That lean is where the season's value comes from. His 109 attempts of 10+ air yards have added 66.7 EPA, more than twice what his 223 short throws have added. The 0.213 EPA per dropback ranks 7th of 55 and is a clear recovery from last year's 16th-ranked 0.157, though it is still short of his 2024 peak.

The early-season version was the best one. In Weeks 2, 5 and 7 he threw into tight windows on a quarter or more of his attempts and posted EPA games of 15.9, 14.8 and 8.1. Starting with the Minnesota game, that aggressiveness collapsed to 4%, 0%, 6.5% and 10.7%, and the efficiency went with it. Over the last five games his EPA per dropback is 0.083 below his season mark. Detroit won all five, but the offense won the Minnesota and Miami games 19-15 and 19-9 and did very little through the air in either.

The numbers hide two things. First, the interception rate. His season 1.2% ranks 12th, but he has historically been a mid-to-high interception passer, and the last three games are already at 3.6%, with a 25.8% bad-throw rate in the New England win. His season bad-throw rate of 15.1% ranks 30th of 45, which is normal for him (2018 and 2022 ranked the same), so a clean interception line was never going to last. Second, third down is a genuine hole: -0.114 EPA a play, a -13.7 CPOE, 9 of his 22 sacks, and a 34.4% conversion rate. The early-down machine is real. The money downs have been bailed out by first- and second-down efficiency.

The Tampa Bay game is the encouraging note. Against the league's No. 3 defense he added 8.9 EPA with his longest average time to throw of the year and the ball back above 8 intended air yards. If that is the template going forward, the midseason slide looks more like a run of grind-it-out game scripts than a decline. The supporting cast still leans downfield: Jameson Williams at 0.479 EPA per target and LaPorta at 0.411 are his two most efficient options.

strengths.title: Intermediate and deep throws carry everything
strengths.body: His 10-19 yard throws return 0.521 EPA each, and his 29 deep attempts return 0.863 with a +9.1 CPOE. This is anticipation throwing from a clean pocket to receivers who win vertically, and it ties directly to the jump in aggressiveness. The skill has held up across his Detroit years. The volume is the question, since he has thrown far fewer tight-window balls since Week 8.

strengths.title: Top-ten efficiency, again
strengths.body: At 0.213 EPA per dropback (7th) and 0.24 above the qualifier average, he is back in the tier he occupied in 2022 and 2024 after a middling 2025. It rests on a supporting cast of St. Brown, Williams and LaPorta, plus an offense that ranks 3rd in pass EPA. With the personnel intact, that level is sustainable.

strengths.title: Red-zone finishing
strengths.body: He has 14 touchdowns and 1 interception on 61 red-zone attempts, which keeps his scoring rate high even as yardage has dipped. The completion rate there is only 59%, so part of this is the offense creating easy looks rather than tight-window brilliance. Expect it to hold reasonably but not at this ratio.

concerns.title: Third downs are a weak spot
concerns.body: On third down his EPA flips to -0.114, his CPOE is -13.7, and 9 of his 22 sacks have come there, facing an average of 7.1 yards to go. A rhythm passer facing obvious passing downs and disguised pressure is the classic weakness for this type, and it runs against his early-down efficiency. Unless the early downs keep producing manageable distances, this will keep stalling drives.

concerns.title: Interceptions catching up
concerns.body: The season interception rate looks clean, but the last three games run at 3.6%, and the bad-throw rate ranks 30th of 45. His career history says the true level is closer to the recent stretch than the season mark, so some regression is likely to continue.

concerns.title: Pressure turns into sacks
concerns.body: He is pressured on only 18.7% of dropbacks (11th lowest), but 31.8% of that pressure ends in a sack (27th of 45), worse than the roughly one-in-four of his last two seasons. Holding the ball a bit longer to chase deeper windows is part of the price. Still, a pocket passer with no scramble outlet will be exposed against a strong pass rush.

trend.note: He was explosive through Week 7, cratered against Minnesota and Miami with negative EPA and almost no aggressive throws, then recovered with 9.0 and 8.9 EPA games. The last-five efficiency still trails the season, and the interceptions have ticked up.

nextGame.headline: Chicago's leaky deep coverage tests whether Goff pushes the ball again
nextGame.body:
Chicago's pass defense is top-ten overall (7th in pass EPA) with an unusual shape. It is the second-stingiest defense on short throws (-0.14 EPA) but 31st on deep balls (0.931 EPA allowed). That is close to the mirror image of Goff's profile: his short game is merely good, and his deep game is the best part of his season. The Bears also have the 2nd-best sack rate, which meets his weakest trait, turning pressure into sacks. The likely game: a few short drives die early, and the big plays decide it if he is willing to hold for the shot. Detroit is a 2.5-point home underdog with a 55.5 total, and the Lions defense ranks 27th, so volume should be there.

On availability, LaPorta (ankle, questionable, limited at Monday's walkthrough) matters most. He is Goff's second-most efficient target, though Chicago holds lead tight ends to -0.02 EPA a target, so the cost may be smaller in this specific matchup. Center Cade Mays is on IR, but he played in only two games, so that thins depth more than it removes a regular. On Chicago's side, corner Kyler Gordon (57% snaps in his four games) is out, which weakens a secondary that already leaks deep. The game is indoors, and Detroit is on four days' rest, the same turnaround as Week 2, when Goff posted his best EPA game of the year in Buffalo.

keyMatchups.title: Deep shots versus a 31st-ranked deep defense
keyMatchups.body: Goff's 0.863 EPA on deep attempts meets a Bears defense allowing 0.931 EPA on deep throws. Williams, at 0.479 EPA per target, is the obvious beneficiary. The only question is whether Detroit calls those shots after a month of conservative throwing.

keyMatchups.title: Bears pass rush versus his sack habit
keyMatchups.body: Chicago's 0.09 sack rate ranks 2nd, and Goff converts pressure to sacks at a bottom-tier rate with almost no scrambling to escape. Expect a couple of drive-killing sacks, especially on third down.

keyMatchups.title: Lead back open as a receiver
keyMatchups.body: Opposing lead backs have outscored their averages against Chicago by 2.5 PPR a game (29th) and post 0.04 EPA a play (30th). Gibbs has been a low-efficiency target this year, but this is the week his checkdowns could turn into real gains against a defense that otherwise smothers the short middle.

nextGame.watch: His early tight-window and deep throws: if Detroit opens with shots at Chicago's soft deep coverage like it did in September, Goff has a 300-yard ceiling; if he keeps checking down into the league's 2nd-best short defense, it looks like Minnesota again.

restOfSeason.body:
The efficiency should land between the early-season and recent versions: roughly top-ten EPA, around 250-285 passing yards a game, and close to two touchdowns per game, driven by an offense that ranks 3rd in pass EPA and a defense poor enough (27th) to keep him throwing. The Tampa Bay game suggests the November dip was partly game script and opponents (Minnesota is the No. 1 defense) rather than decline.

What regresses is the interception rate. His history and his bad-throw rate point to more turnovers than his season line shows, and something like 0.5-0.9 a game is a fair expectation. The third-down and pressure-to-sack issues are likely to persist, since they fit who he is. LaPorta's ankle is the main threat to the efficiency, because he and Williams are the targets who make the intermediate and deep game work.

confidence.note: Ten starts fit his career profile, but the recent drop in aggressiveness, small deep sample and LaPorta's status leave real uncertainty.
